title: Stock cover at the end of December 2024

brief.decision: Which store and product pairs get stock first in the replenishment run, based on the weeks of stock left on 29 December 2024 at a sales rate that out-of-stock days do not pull down

expected_output.grain: one row per store and product with less than 2 weeks of cover on 29 December 2024

checkpoints.prompt: Yara needs a weekly sales rate for each store and product over 1 to 28 December 2024, and some shelves stood at 0 units on several of those days. Which days should the weekly rate be worked out over?

options.text: Every day of the 28-day window, with a day of no sales counted as 0 units, whatever the shelf held that day
Only the days with at least one sale, since a day with no sale says nothing about demand
The days whose closing stock is above 0, with a day of no sales on them counted as 0 units
Every day of December 2024, all 31 of them, so that the rate covers the whole month

checkpoints.prompt: Yara first wants to know how many shelves ran out. Take each store's closing stock of each product per day, for every store and product with daily stock figures, from 1 to 28 December 2024, both days included. How many store and product pairs closed at least one of those days with 0 units on hand? Count each pair once. Type a whole number.
Write the query that answers Yara's question.

Yara's headline: how many store and product pairs would a sales rate over every day of the window leave off the list of pairs with less than 2 weeks of cover? Take every store and product with daily closing stock figures, and the units the store sold of that product on its own store orders (channel 'store'), each order counted on the UTC date of its order_ts, which holds UTC time, from 1 to 28 December 2024, both days included; a day with no sale counts as 0 units. An in-stock day is a day of that window whose closing stock is above 0. The in-stock rate is 7 times the units sold on in-stock days divided by the number of in-stock days; the every-day rate is 7 times the units sold over all 28 days divided by 28. A pair's weeks of cover at a rate is its closing stock on 29 December 2024 divided by that rate, unrounded. Leave out a pair with no in-stock day or no units sold on its in-stock days. Count the pairs whose cover is less than 2 weeks at the in-stock rate but 2 weeks or more at the every-day rate. Type a whole number.

Yara's list holds the store and product pairs with less than 2 weeks of cover on 29 December 2024, each at its weekly sales rate over its in-stock days from 1 to 28 December 2024. Some of the pairs are PlayBox 5 consoles, which were out of stock for most of December and were refilled on 28 December. What can Yara take from the list?

options.text: Each pair on the list will run out within 2 weeks, so every one of them needs a delivery today, with PlayBox 5 first in line.
Which pairs run out within 2 weeks if December's in-stock rate holds; PlayBox 5's rate rests on a few gift-season days, and stock on order is left out.
The PlayBox 5 pairs are listed only because of their stockout, so a rate over every day of the window would be the fairer and steadier measure to use for them.
That the pairs left off the list are safe for January, since none of them ran short of stock on any day of December.

checkpoints.prompt: Write 2 to 4 sentences for Yara: which store and product pairs need stock first and why, how the out-of-stock days changed their sales rate, one caveat about a rate taken from December, and one next step before tomorrow's replenishment run.

model_plan:
Metric formula: avg_weekly_units = 7 times the units sold on in-stock days divided by the number of in-stock days, rounded to 2 decimals; weeks_cover = the closing stock on 29 December 2024 divided by the unrounded weekly rate, rounded to 1 decimal; keep the pairs under 2 weeks before rounding.
Output grain: one row per store and product with less than 2 weeks of cover.
Tables and keys: inventory_chain_daily (one row per day, store and product) as the date spine for 1 to 28 December 2024, left joined to each day's store units from orders and order_lines on store_id, product_id and the UTC order date; its 29 December 2024 rows joined on store_id and product_id for the stock.
Filters: store orders only (channel 'store'); order dates and stock days from 1 to 28 December 2024; stock on 29 December 2024.
Edge cases: a day with no sale has no sales row, so it is filled with 0 rather than dropped; a day closing at 0 leaves the rate even when the stock left without a sale, as a return to the supplier; a pair with no in-stock day or no units sold is left out; order lines are added up per day before the join, so a day with two lines is not counted twice.
Expected row count: 8
model_answer_template: On 29 December 2024 the list holds the store and product pairs with less than 2 weeks of cover, and {CP4} of them would look safe at a rate over every day of the window, because their shelves stood at 0 for much of December and hid their demand. {CP2} store and product pairs closed at least one day of the window out of stock, all of them PlayBox 5, whose rate now rests on a few in-stock days of the gift season, so it may overstate January demand. Next, I would check the deliveries already on order for these pairs and move stock from stores with plenty of cover before tomorrow's run.
follow_up_question: Which of these pairs should get stock first, and can any of it come from stores with more cover?
